newsitem.title: UK: Europe oil industry won't succumb to merger mania.
newsitem.headline: Europe oil industry won't succumb to merger mania.

text.p: The proposed merger of the U.S. refining and marketing sectors of two Western oil majors is unlikely to trigger a wave of similar high-profile marriages in Europe's downstream sector, industry analysts said.
The proposed $10 billion tie-up between Shell Oil and Texaco comes hot on the heels of a deal worth $5 billion to merge the European refining and retail sectors of British Petroleum and Mobil.
But industry-watchers believe that the European operations of BP and Mobil are a rare strategic fit.
"I would be very surprised to see another merger of two major players on that scale," said Mathieu Zajdela, head of studies at Paris-based energy consultants Enerfinance.
Indeed, at the announcement of the BP/Mobil merger, BP chief executive John Browne said that the two companies' operations were "uniquely complementary".

The profitability of Europe's downstream oil sector is at an all-time low as dwindling retail margins in the continent's major markets combine with already-weak refining margins resulting from chronic overcapacity.
But experts believe that so-called megamergers are not the answer to the industry's woes.
"A merger isn't a catch-all solution for the industry's fundamental structural problems," one oil company analyst said.
"When you combine weak resources, low quality assets in both refining and marketing, you don't make a strong company," said Zadjela.

It was a different story for BP and Mobil which have refineries in all the key locations and a good match of filling station networks, giving potential for significant economies of scale, analysts said.
"If you run 500 service stations, it's not much of a bigger deal to run 1,000," said Zadjela.
And both companies are strong in regions where oil product demand is growing rapidly, especially in Portugal, Spain, Greece and Italy.

But in general, the scope for cost-cutting in the European downstream sector through a giant merger may be limited, as most companies have already pared costs to the bone by slashing staffing levels and expensive storage capacity to a bare minimum.
The real issue is ridding the European refining sector of the massive overcapacity, of up to 60 million tonnes a year, that is cramping profits, analysts believe.

"The problem of the European downstream is really a problem of margins rather than costs, but (a merger) could help if it involved a rationalisation of refining capacity, said Gordon Gray, an oil industry analyst at Salomon Brothers.
But having dismissed megamergers, industry-watchers see a brighter future for smaller, local alliances focused on retailing.
"A lot can be done in terms of local cooperation, particularly in terms of transport and storage," said Zajdela.
Certain markets such as the U.K. are crying out for such alliances to help oil companies overcome fierce competition from cut-price supermarket forecourts.
And one aspect of the proposed Shell/Texaco deal which particularly appeals to industry analysts is the tie-in of the giant oil producer Saudi Aramco.
"Some of the European companies that are the most fragile may find cooperation with producers a good way to secure their future," said a London-based analyst.
